concepts.topicTitle: Nature and Systems of Social Science in Daily Life
concepts.label: What Social Science Is
concepts.cardText: Human beings live in societies and depend on each other in many ways. Our lives are shaped by the environment, the institutions that govern us, the economic activities that meet our needs, and the traditions and ideas passed down through generations. Understanding these connections is the foundation of Social Science. In simple words, Social Science is the systematic study of human society. It tells us not only what happened or where things are located, but also why events occur, how people live together, how environments influence life, how governments function, how economies operate, and how the past and present shape the world. While Physics, Chemistry and Biology study the natural world, Social Science focuses on society, institutions, cultures and human interactions.

concepts.topicTitle: Nature and Systems of Social Science in Daily Life
concepts.label: Social Science in Everyday Life: Society Does Not Function by Chance
concepts.cardText: Think about a day in your life. You wake up in a house built with materials from different places. The food you eat may come from various regions, and before it reaches your plate it has been harvested, processed, transported, bought and sold by many people. You travel on roads planned and maintained by public authorities, study in a school shaped by educational policies, and use electricity generated at distant power stations and delivered through a vast network. Even the simplest daily activities rely on systems of governance, economic production, social cooperation and the natural environment. Questions about crowded cities, different languages, farming regions or floods show that society does not function by chance: it is shaped by history, geography, institutions, resources and human choices.

concepts.topicTitle: Indian Knowledge Traditions, Environment and Ethical Governance
concepts.label: Understanding Society Through Time and Traditions
concepts.cardText: Society has not always been as it is today; over thousands of years it has changed greatly. Early communities depended directly on nature and learnt to grow crops, domesticate animals, build settlements, develop tools, exchange goods and organise governance. This spirit of inquiry has deep roots in India's knowledge traditions, where early thinkers valued discussion, questioning and logical reasoning. The Pañchamahābhūtas describes the natural world as an interconnected system in which human life is embedded, and the idea of vasudhaiva kuṭumbakam, 'the world is one family', expresses the interconnectedness of human societies. Early reflections on governance, such as the Arthaśhāstra attributed to Kauṭilya about 2,300 years ago, linked political authority with public welfare and ethical responsibility. Social scientists observe people's lives, conduct interviews and surveys, examine documents and compare times and places, developing explanations supported by evidence.

concepts.topicTitle: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Methodologies in Social Science
concepts.label: Social Science as a Group of Disciplines
concepts.cardText: Human society is complex and no single field of study can fully explain it. A drought, for example, affects crops (environment), farmers' incomes (economy), government relief measures (politics), migration to cities (society) and traditional ways of coping with scarcity (culture). So Social Science is not a single subject but a group of related disciplines, each focusing on a different aspect of human life. In Grades 9 to 10 it primarily draws from four core disciplines: Geography, History, Political Science and Economics. Sociology, Philosophy, Anthropology and Psychology also form part of the broader family. Geography studies the Earth, its environments and the relationships between people and their surroundings; History examines the human past and how societies change; Political Science analyses systems of governance, power, and rights and responsibilities; Economics explores how societies produce, distribute and utilise resources.

concepts.topicTitle: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Methodologies in Social Science
concepts.label: Geography and History: Tools, Sources and Methods
concepts.cardText: Geography studies the location and distribution of places, objects, materials and people, and the relationships between human societies and their surroundings. It seeks to understand where things are, why they are found there, and how places affect one another over time, combining spatial and temporal perspectives. It uses maps, globes, atlases, GIS, infographics and other tools. History is the study of the human past, through which societies understand people's experiences, values and changes over time. Modern historiography relies increasingly on empirical evidence and tools such as carbon-14 dating and archaeology. Sources include literary sources such as travelogues, memoirs, folklore and revenue documents; archaeological sources such as monuments, artefacts and sculptures; epigraphic sources, inscriptions on durable materials; and numismatic sources, coins and currency.

concepts.topicTitle: Interdisciplinary Perspectives and Methodologies in Social Science
concepts.label: Political Science and Economics
concepts.cardText: Political Science is the study of governance: how and why power is distributed, decisions are made and policies implemented. It studies constitutions, governments and institutions, as well as social movements, nation building and foreign policy. In India's villages, the Panchayati Raj system embodies grassroots democracy by giving citizens a voice in local development planning. Indian political thought linked politics with dharma (moral duty), artha (economic well-being) and rājadharma (the duties of the ruler); the Arthaśhāstra is a foundational text on politics and administration, and power was viewed as a responsibility rather than merely a privilege. Economics helps us understand how individuals and societies decide how to use limited resources to meet their needs, studying how goods and services are produced, exchanged and distributed, and the decisions of consumers, producers and governments.

concepts.topicTitle: Civic Responsibility, Democratic Decision-Making and Future Outlook
concepts.label: Why We Should Study Social Science
concepts.cardText: The house you live in, the water you use, the roads you travel on, the school you attend and even the digital spaces you use are part of systems created and managed by society. Social Science helps us understand how these systems developed, how they function and how they affect different groups. People speak different languages, follow diverse customs and practise varied occupations; Social Science explains such variations as outcomes of geographical, historical, cultural and economic factors, which builds respect and cooperation, while Indian culture binds diversity together through an underlying unity. In a democratic society citizens play an active role, and understanding how governments function prepares us to participate responsibly. It also strengthens our ability to ask informed questions about shared challenges such as environmental protection, public health, employment or urban growth, and connects the past, present and future.

concepts.topicTitle: Civic Responsibility, Democratic Decision-Making and Future Outlook
concepts.label: The Future of Social Science and the Two-Year Journey
concepts.cardText: As societies change rapidly, the importance of Social Science continues to grow. New technologies, expanding cities, environmental concerns, migration and global connections are reshaping how people live, and understanding them requires careful observation, asking questions, examining evidence and recognising connections. Social Science will help societies address climate change, sustainable development, social harmony and equitable use of resources, and guide the responsible use of new technologies. It prepares you not only to understand the world but to take part in shaping it as informed and thoughtful citizens. Social Science is not about memorising dates, maps or definitions; it is about understanding people, places, society, culture and power. Over Grades 9–10 you will explore history, geography, political systems and economies, learning to analyse evidence, compare perspectives and see how past, present and future are linked.
